title: Running a stand-up
examples: How long should my opening joke be?
What is the best way to structure a 10-minute set?
If I go over time, what should I do?

explain.say: Today we are looking at the structure of a comedy set.
A good format usually has a clear beginning and end.
Timeboxing means keeping every section within a set time limit.
For example, if you have ten minutes, the closer should take about two minutes.
In real life, think about a presentation you must give at work.
A common mistake is spending too much time on the setup material.

faq.q: How do I know if my format is working?
faq.a: You can test this by running the material for friends first. They will give you feedback on pacing and structure. You might also ask, 'How do I test if my jokes have a clear beginning and end?' or 'What makes a good joke format?'
asks: How do I structure my jokes?
What is the best flow for stand-up?

faq.q: What if I run out of time during my set?
faq.a: It is better to end strong than to run over time. You should always have one or two solid, short bits ready as backups. You could also ask, 'What if I finish early?' or 'How do I cut my set if I am too long?'
asks: What to do if I go over time?

faq.q: Is there a specific ratio for the sections?
faq.a: While there is no hard rule, a general guideline is to dedicate the most time to your strongest material. The opening should grab attention quickly, and the closer should leave a lasting impact. You might ask, 'Should the middle be the longest part?' or 'Is there a time ratio I must follow?'
asks: What percentage of time should I use?
How much time for each part?

faq.q: Does timeboxing apply to non-comedy speaking?
faq.a: Yes, timeboxing is a useful skill for any professional speaking engagement. It helps you allocate attention across different topics evenly. You could ask, 'Does this help with work presentations?' or 'Can I use this for speeches?'

faq.q: What is the difference between format and structure?
faq.a: Format refers to the overall expected shape, like a three-act play. Structure refers to the specific arrangement of jokes within that shape. You might ask, 'Are these words the same?' or 'What is the difference between the two?'

facts: A standard comedy set often follows a three-part structure: opening, body, and closer.
Timeboxing requires allocating specific, limited amounts of time to different segments of your talk.
The opening section should aim to capture the audience's attention immediately.
The closer should be your strongest material to leave a positive final impression.

quiz.say: If you have a ten minute set, and your best material is worth seven minutes, what should the remaining time be used for?
quiz.show: 10 min set: 1 min opening, 7 min middle, 2 min closer

options.show: Using the remaining time to repeat jokes.
options.say: Using the remaining time to repeat jokes.

options.show: Spending all the time on the best material.
options.say: Spending all the time on the best material.

options.show: Making the opening and closing equal.
options.say: Making the opening and closing equal.

quiz.why: The structure requires time for the beginning and the end, which together make up the remaining time.

wrong.0: Repetition wastes valuable time and makes the material feel padded.
wrong.2: This leaves no time for the necessary opening hook or a strong conclusion.
wrong.3: While balance is nice, the closer should often be weighted more heavily than the opening.

quiz.say: When timeboxing a presentation, what is the primary goal of the opening section?

options.show: To read the entire document aloud.
options.say: To read the entire document aloud.

options.show: To immediately hook the audience's interest.
options.say: To immediately hook the audience's interest.

options.show: To cover all the background information.
options.say: To cover all the background information.

quiz.why: The opening must prove to the audience right away that listening to you is worthwhile.

wrong.0: Apologizing draws attention to nerves, which distracts from your actual message.
wrong.1: Reading prevents you from connecting with the audience through natural speaking.
wrong.3: This is too much detail and will cause the audience to lose focus before you start.

quiz.say: If you are giving a 20 minute talk, and you feel you need more material, where is the safest place to add it?

options.show: The middle section, as it has the most time allocated.
options.say: The middle section, as it has the most time allocated.

quiz.why: The middle section is the largest part of the set, giving you the most flexibility to expand without risking the impact of the opening or closing.

wrong.1: Too much early material can bore the audience before you even get to your best points.
wrong.2: Adding too much material to the end can dilute the punch and weaken the final impact.
wrong.3: Random additions disrupt the natural flow and rhythm of the entire performance.
